name: Time-series databases
summary: A database shaped for measurements stamped with time.
howItWorks: Time-series databases are built for data that arrives as timestamp, source and value, and is almost always appended rather than updated. They split data into time chunks, compress old chunks heavily, and keep pre-computed rollups so questions like “hourly average for the last 30 days” stay fast. Retention policies drop or downsample old data automatically, which also stops queries that forget a time range from growing without end.
analogy: A ship’s logbook with a fresh page every day. Recent pages lie open on the desk; old volumes get summarized and shelved.
useWhen: IoT and sensor telemetry, infrastructure metrics, market ticks
Dashboards over recent windows plus long-term trends
High ingest rates where rows are rarely changed
avoidWhen: Transactional business data with frequent updates
Data you don’t mainly query by time
example: Pressure readings from thousands of wells land every few seconds in a TimescaleDB hypertable. The live chart reads the last 15 minutes, and a continuous aggregate keeps hourly averages, so a one-year chart reads 8,760 rows instead of millions.

providers.aws: Timestream for InfluxDB (Timestream for LiveAnalytics has been closed to new customers since June 2025)
providers.oss: TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, Prometheus, QuestDB, TDengine (IoT, one table per device), Apache IoTDB (industrial IoT; path tree or SQL tables over TsFile), GreptimeDB (metrics, logs and traces on object storage), Arc (DuckDB and Parquet), ArcticDB (Man Group; versioned pandas DataFrames on S3 or LMDB; source-available BSL); proprietary: kdb+ (KX, free Community Edition), used widely in finance

source: CREATE TABLE readings (time timestamptz NOT NULL, well_id int, psi double precision);
-- hourly rollup, refreshed every hour by a background policy
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW readings_hourly WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS
SELECT time_bucket('1 hour', time) AS hour, well_id, avg(psi) AS avg_psi
FROM readings GROUP BY hour, well_id;
start_offset => INTERVAL '3 hours', end_offset => INTERVAL '1 hour',

diagram.caption: Readings are appended in time order. The live chart reads each new row almost at once, while the rollup job wakes periodically and summarizes a batch.

story: Time-series storage grew out of network monitoring. In late 1997 Tobias Oetiker started RRDtool as a successor to his MRTG traffic grapher, and by 1999 it was in public beta, storing measurements such as network bandwidth, machine-room temperature and server load. Its round-robin database gave each series a fixed number of slots, overwrote the oldest values, and kept extra archives that consolidated older points into averages, minimums and maximums, so storage never grew but detail faded with age. That trade-off survives in today’s retention and downsampling policies.

As fleets of servers grew, so did the metrics. Graphite, built at Orbitz by Chris Davis, was open-sourced in 2008. SoundCloud started Prometheus in 2012 because its monitoring, mostly based on StatsD and Graphite, couldn’t keep up with hundreds of microservices, and InfluxDB followed in 2013. Facebook’s 2015 Gorilla paper showed how far compression could go: by storing timestamps as differences of differences and values XORed with the previous one, it cut storage about tenfold, enough to keep recent metrics in memory.

Others went back to SQL. TimescaleDB, launched in 2017, argued that relational databases handle time series well once the scaling problem is solved, and runs as a PostgreSQL extension. Cloud providers added managed services, such as Amazon Timestream, generally available in September 2020.

choices.why: RRDtool’s circular buffer kept the storage footprint constant over time. Recent data stayed at full resolution and older data survived only as consolidated averages, minimums and maximums.

New points almost always land in the latest interval, and queries ask for time ranges. Splitting data into time chunks keeps the active chunk small and fast, and dropping old data means deleting whole chunks.

Timestamps arrive at regular intervals and values change little between readings, so encoding only the change saves a lot: Gorilla stored about 96% of timestamps in a single bit and shrank each 16-byte point to 1.37 bytes on average. Gorilla’s authors also noted that users care about aggregates and recent data more than individual old points.
Prometheus made a multi-dimensional data model a design goal: each series is a metric name plus key-value labels, so one query can slice by host, region or service.

timeline.text: Tobias Oetiker’s RRDtool, with its fixed-size round-robin database, is in public beta
Graphite, built at Orbitz, is open-sourced

TimescaleDB brings time-series storage to PostgreSQL
